Z.notes: All 25 of its tests pass. It has the cleanest design: commands are pure (data, args) -> {data, out} functions, and main loads and saves exactly once (todo.mjs:68-113). reasoning:
All three solutions pass their own tests and meet every explicit spec line in my probes, so the ranking turns on robustness, test depth and polish.

X is first. It has the strongest data validation (it rejects duplicate ids and ids at or above nextId) and by far the most thorough test suite. That suite is 95 cases, built from matrices of corrupt contents and bad ids, plus tests for numeric sorting, prototype-key commands, non-ASCII text and leftover temp files. Its only real flaw is a raw stack trace on unexpected I/O errors, and Z has the same flaw.

Z is second. It has the best architecture (pure command functions with a single load/save point), the best README, and a careful 25-test suite. Against that, its shape check is weak: a hand-edited file with a null todo crashes it, and a stale lastId can produce duplicate ids. It also reads the data file before validating arguments.

Y is third. Its core code is essentially X's, and it handles I/O errors the most gracefully of the three. But it has the weakest test deliverable: 12 compact tests that never clean up their temp dirs, never check that setup steps succeeded, and skip numeric sorting and the edge-case ids. It also uses bare exit-code numbers and has no duplicate-id check. Z's much stronger tests, docs and structure outweigh Y's edge in robustness on inputs outside the spec.

X.notes: Strengths: meets every spec line in my probes. add joins then trims, ids come from a persisted nextId so they are never reused, list sorts numerically, done is idempotent, invalid id gives exit 2 and missing id gives exit 1, clear-done reports its count, usage goes to stderr with exit 2, and a corrupt file exits 3 with the file untouched. It has the strongest data validation of the three (todo.mjs:31-40): it checks each todo's types, rejects duplicate ids, and requires every id to be below nextId. A hand-edited file therefore cannot produce garbage output or id collisions. The atomic write uses a hidden temp file in the same folder, named with pid and Date.now(), and cleans it up on failure (todo.mjs:61-70). Object.hasOwn guards prototype keys, there are named exit-code constants, and it uses process.exitCode rather than process.exit. Tests: 95 passing. Every corrupt-shape case is crossed with every command and checks that the file is unchanged and no temp file is left. Each invalid-id form ('', ' 1', 0x1, 1e2, 1.5) is checked, and so are the -1 and missing-file not-found cases, numeric versus lexicographic sort, non-ASCII text, and __proto__/toString as commands. Temp dirs are cleaned in afterEach and NODE_TEST_CONTEXT is stripped from the child env. Defects: unexpected I/O errors are rethrown as raw stack traces (todo.mjs:130). For example, TODO_FILE pointing at a directory, or into a missing parent folder, dumps a node:fs stack. Huge ids lose precision ('9007199254740993' becomes '#9007199254740992'; there is no safe-integer check, and the other two share this). Formatting nit at todo.mjs:29 (`dataFile =() =>`). The README is accurate and concise but never says that valid JSON with the wrong shape is also reported as corrupt.

Y.notes: Strengths: all spec behaviours were correct in my probes. It uses a persisted nextId, the same-folder temp file plus rename (todo.mjs:46-55), and full per-todo shape validation including id < nextId (todo.mjs:38-41). It validates text and id before loading the file. It is the only solution that turns unexpected I/O errors into a friendly 'Error: ...' line with exit 1 instead of a stack trace (todo.mjs:121-122), for example EISDIR, or ENOENT on a missing parent folder. The code is compact and readable, and Object.hasOwn guards prototype keys. Tests: 12 passing and they cover each spec bullet, including bad-shape JSON, the default todo.json in cwd, no leftover temp files, and 0x1/1.5/'' ids. Defects: the tests are thin next to the other two. They never check leading zeros, -1, out-of-order stored todos, done/remove on a missing file, or that invalid-id and not-found leave the file unchanged. Several assertions check only .out or .code, so stderr is not asserted (test lines 29, 34). The mkdtemp directories are never removed (beforeEach has no matching cleanup), and the env inherits process.env wholesale. Duplicate ids in a hand-edited file are not detected (X does detect them). The 'Error: ' prefix is repeated in every CliError message instead of being added in one place. The I/O error message leaks the full temp path, which is acceptable for a local CLI. README: the exit-code table says 3 means 'not valid JSON' but bad shapes also give 3. It is otherwise accurate and terse, with no example of TODO_FILE use.

Its only notable gap is that app.js DOM rendering is untested; only the fetch logic is tested, which is what the spec requires.

Z ranks second. It is equally spec-compliant, including non-ASCII URLs, and is equally hardened: early 413, nosniff, CSP, graceful shutdown. It also tests DOM rendering. Its tests miss several boundaries that X covers, its http.mjs module mixes unrelated concerns, and its README is thinner.

It also reads an entire oversized body before replying 413, with no Content-Length pre-check; a request declaring 50000 bytes hung in the probe. reasoning:
Z and Y are close, and both are clearly better than X.

Z ranks first on correctness and robustness. It accepts every valid absolute http(s) URL, including non-ASCII paths and IDN hosts, and redirects to the exact stored string, encoding only when the header would otherwise be invalid. It also rejects oversized uploads early using Content-Length while still delivering the 413 cleanly, and adds CSP and nosniff headers. Its code is the most compact, and its frontend design (init(doc, fetch) plus exported render functions) is the easiest to test.

Y has the best tests (149, with process-level checks of defaults and invalid PORT, and a precise rolling-window test with mock timers) and the best README. However, it rejects legitimate non-ASCII and IDN URLs with 400, reads a whole oversized body before sending 413, retries code generation without a bound, and has slightly less modular server code. Those spec and edge-case gaps outweigh its test and doc advantages by a small margin.

X is well structured, but it has two verified behaviour defects. First, it always normalises the Location header, so 'https://example.com' redirects to 'https://example.com/', breaking 'Location set to the stored url' and contradicting its README. Second, it fails to drain large declared bodies, which gives clients ECONNRESET instead of 413 for most bodies of 64 KB or more. Its tests also miss both bugs and leave the DOM rendering in app.js untested.
